title: When an instruction needs a result that is not ready
objective: By the end of this lesson you can identify a data hazard in a short instruction sequence, explain what forwarding does about it, and measure on your own machine what a dependency chain costs.

blocks.text: The pipeline picture assumed each instruction could proceed every cycle. Here is a sequence where it cannot.

blocks.caption: The second instruction needs what the first has not yet written
lines: add  x5, x6, x7      # produces x5
sub  x9, x5, x8      # needs x5
cycle:       1     2     3     4     5     6
add        | IF  | ID  | EX  | MEM | WB  |
sub              | IF  | ID  | EX  | ...
|     the sub reads x5 here, in cycle 3
the add writes x5 here, in cycle 5
The sub reads the register file two cycles before the add writes to it.
Without a remedy it would read the old value of x5 and be wrong.

blocks.title: This is called a data hazard
blocks.text: An instruction needs a value that an earlier, still-in-flight instruction is going to produce. It is a hazard of the pipeline itself: the same two instructions executed one at a time have no problem, because the first completes entirely before the second starts. Overlapping created the difficulty, so overlapping has to solve it.
Forwarding: use the value before it is stored

Look at the timing again. The add computes the sum in cycle 3, during its execute stage. The sub needs it in cycle 4, at the start of its own execute stage. The value exists a full cycle before it is needed — it is simply not in the register file yet. Forwarding adds a path that routes the result straight from the output of the arithmetic unit back to its input, skipping the write and the read entirely.

blocks.caption: The forwarding path
lines: |     forwarding path       |
v                           |
registers -> [ arithmetic unit ] -----------+---> memory -> registers
|                      result available here
the sub takes its input
from the path, not from
the register file
/* The register file still gets written. Forwarding does not replace it,
it only lets the next instruction skip the wait. */

blocks.text: With forwarding, this hazard costs nothing at all: the sub proceeds in the cycle it was scheduled for. Most back-to-back arithmetic dependencies are handled this way, which is why an ordinary sequence of dependent arithmetic still runs at close to one instruction per cycle.

blocks.title: Forwarding removes the stall, not the dependency
blocks.text: The sub still cannot start before the add produces its value — that ordering is what the program means. Forwarding shortens the wait from three cycles to zero for arithmetic. What it cannot do is make a dependent chain run in parallel with itself, and that limit is measurable.
What a dependency chain actually costs

A modern processor issues several instructions per cycle when they do not depend on each other. Two loops doing exactly the same number of additions — one as a single chain where each add needs the previous result, one as four separate chains — show what that is worth. The values are kept in registers so nothing here is about memory.

blocks.caption: Measured on an Apple M-series processor, best of repeated runs
lines: identical total additions (400,000,000), values never leave registers
1 dependent chain    :  0.185 s   0.46 ns per add
4 independent chains :  0.048 s   0.12 ns per add
ratio                :  3.85x
/* The same number of additions. The four-chain loop finished in a quarter
of the time because nothing in it had to wait for anything else. */

blocks.text: Four times the work per unit of time, from nothing but breaking one chain into four. The processor was never four times faster; it was idle three quarters of the time in the first loop, waiting for each addition to finish before the next could start.
Why this matters when you write ordinary code

headers: What it does to the processor
rows: One chain; each addition waits for the previous
Four partial sums added at the end
A chain by construction; the next address comes from the current node
Addresses are known in advance and do not form a chain

blocks.text: This is the mechanical reason an array outperforms a linked list even when both fit in cache and both touch the same number of elements. The array is not merely more compact — its addresses are independent, so the processor can have many loads in flight. The list forces one at a time. Cache behaviour makes the gap larger still, and that is the subject of the memory module.

blocks.title: The compiler does this for you, when it is allowed to
blocks.text: Breaking one floating-point sum into several partial sums changes the result, because floating-point addition is not associative — the rounding lesson in the C course showed why. So a compiler will not do it to floating-point code unless you tell it that reassociation is acceptable. For integers it is free, and compilers do it routinely. When a floating-point loop seems stuck at a fixed rate no matter the optimisation level, a single accumulator is a good first suspect.

blocks.title: Measure your own machine
steps: Write a loop that adds 1 to a single variable 400 million times, and time it. The course never showed how to time C code, so here it is:
static double now(void) { struct timespec t; clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &t);
double t0 = now();  /* ... the loop ... */  double elapsed = now() - t0;
Use CLOCK_MONOTONIC, not time() — it does not jump when the system clock is adjusted
Write a second loop with four separate variables, 100 million iterations each
Compile at -O1 or higher and check the timings
If either time is 0.000 s, the compiler deleted the loop — verify with: cc -O2 -S -o - prog.c | grep -c add
Prevent deletion with an empty asm barrier: __asm__ volatile("" : "+r"(a));
Re-measure and record the ratio between the two loops
Try eight chains instead of four and see whether the ratio keeps improving
Explain what the point where it stops improving tells you about the processor
blocks.expected: A ratio near the number of instructions the processor can issue per cycle, and a point beyond which more chains stop helping. On the machine used above, four chains gave exactly 3.85x and that is the useful measurement: it did not come from a specification sheet, it came from a loop you can run. The deleted-loop step is not optional — an unexplained 0.000 s is always the optimiser, never a fast processor.

cheatsheet: A data hazard: an instruction needs a value an earlier in-flight instruction has not written yet
Executed one at a time the same instructions have no hazard — overlapping created it
Forwarding routes the result from the arithmetic unit output back to its input
For back-to-back arithmetic, forwarding removes the stall entirely
Forwarding removes the wait, not the dependency: a chain still runs one step at a time
Measured: 1 dependent chain 0.46 ns per add, 4 independent chains 0.12 ns — 3.85x
Array indices are independent addresses; linked-list addresses form a chain
Compilers split integer accumulators freely, floating-point ones only with permission
A timing of 0.000 s means the optimiser deleted the loop, not that it was fast

checkpoint.prompt: add x5,x6,x7 is followed immediately by sub x9,x5,x8. What is the problem in a pipelined processor?

choices.A: Two instructions cannot use the arithmetic unit
choices.B: The registers are the wrong size
choices.D: The sub reads the register file before the add has written its result there

checkpoint.explanation: The sub reads in cycle 3 and the add writes in cycle 5. Without a remedy the sub reads the stale value of x5.

checkpoint.prompt: How does forwarding fix that without slowing anything down?

choices.A: It delays the sub until the write completes
choices.D: The result exists at the arithmetic unit's output a cycle before it is needed

checkpoint.explanation: A path routes it directly to the input. The value is computed in cycle 3 and needed in cycle 4. It is not late, it is merely not in the register file yet — so the path skips the register file.

checkpoint.prompt: Four independent addition chains ran 3.85x faster than one chain doing the same total additions. What does that show?

choices.A: The compiler removed work from the four-chain version
choices.C: The processor can issue several independent instructions per cycle, and a single chain leaves most of that capacity idle

checkpoint.explanation: Identical work, four times the rate. The single chain was not slow because additions are slow; it was slow because each one had to wait for the previous.

checkpoint.prompt: Why will a compiler split an integer accumulator into several partial sums but refuse to do the same for floating-point?

choices.C: It does the same for both

checkpoint.explanation: Regrouping changes the result. Regrouping is exactly the reassociation the C course's rounding lesson warned about. It is a legal transformation for integers and a change in results for floating-point.
